heading_en: Adjustments of Ruby with Length Longer than that of the Base Characters
heading_ja: ルビが親文字よりはみ出した場合の処理

cases.quote: Ruby text shall not hang over the ideographic characters (cl-19) adjacent to the base characters.
cases.rationale: Rule 1 states a prohibition and no amount: the base characters must be pushed apart by a mono-ruby reading's own excess before composition begins, wherever the neighbor the excess would otherwise overhang resolves to cl-19, and not otherwise (`docs/decisions/mono-ruby-separation-split.md`). Two mono-ruby constructs, each with a one-character reading wider than its own base's supplied advance by an identical 300 units (base 1000, reading 1300): construct 0 sits over item 0 (き), whose only real neighbor, item 1 (あ), is hiragana (cl-15) — no separation is forced. Construct 1 sits over item 3 (か), whose left neighbor, item 2 (鬼), is ideographic (cl-19) — a separation is forced at the boundary between them, item 3 having no right neighbor to force a second one. `lower.separations` is the *complete* list `Contribution::separations` reports across every construct the case declares, compared by count as well as content (`cases.schema.json`'s own `lower.separations` description), so the single declared entry below asserts both halves of the quoted sentence at once: that the boundary after item 2 carries a forced separation, and that the case's own equally oversized construct 0 forces none anywhere — an implementation that fired a separation beside construct 0's own hiragana neighbor, or omitted the one beside construct 1's cl-19 neighbor, fails this case either way. `least` is deliberately not stated: rule 1 states only the prohibition, never an amount, and the amount `lower` computes here is `docs/decisions/mono-ruby-separation-split.md`'s own reading of the arithmetic rather than a fact JLReq states (the companion `unstated`-standing case below is where that reading is asserted, under the standing that names it a reading rather than a requirement).

permitted.source: §3.3.8 rule 1, applied identically under every policy this workspace generates: the prohibition names no question

forbidden.why: Rule 1 forbids ruby from overhanging an adjacent cl-19 character; construct 1's reading is 300 units wider than its own base and its left neighbor (item 2, 鬼) is cl-19, so a boundary carrying no forced separation at all leaves that excess resting on the neighbor rule 1 forbids it from resting on. `construct` is stated explicitly and not left to default to 0: the case asks about construct 1 (the permitted entry's own first-stated `construct`), and an unstated `construct` here would silently forbid a different occurrence's answer, `check_ordinal`'s own mismatch making this entry inert rather than a check on the construct rule 1 actually governs.

cases.quote: Ruby text shall not hang over the ideographic characters (cl-19) adjacent to the base characters.
cases.rationale: Rule 1 states the prohibition; it states no amount and no side for the surplus a mono-ruby run's excess forces apart, which is exactly `docs/decisions/mono-ruby-separation-split.md`'s own silence — three narrower questions the rule's own wording leaves open. This case exercises question 1: how one run's own excess divides between its two boundaries when both neighbors are cl-19. One mono-ruby construct over item 1 (門) of 鬼門河 — 鬼 and 河, items 0 and 2, are both ideographic (cl-19) — carries a reading 3 units wider than its own 1000-unit base, an odd surplus `jlreq_unit::distribute(surplus, &[1, 1], policy.remainder())` cannot split evenly between the two boundaries, so which one carries the extra unit is exactly the tie-break `jlreq_spec::Question::ADJUSTMENT_REMAINDER` already answers for every other proportional split in this workspace, read here for the first time over this construct's own two forced separations. `Policy::JLREQ`'s own default, `RemainderRule::Leading`, gives the leading boundary (after item 0) the extra unit — 2 against 1 — which is the reading this workspace's own default run measures; `RemainderRule::Trailing` gives it to the trailing boundary instead — 1 against 2 — published as a statement to an implementation that declares that alternative, on `3.6.2/center-tab-alignment`'s own identical precedent for the same policy question over a different construct. Neither reading is JLReq's own requirement, which is exactly why this case's own standing is `unstated` and not `normative`: asserting one split as the rule's own requirement would be the §E.2#11 error, measuring kumihan's own bookkeeping choice rather than anything the quoted sentence decides.

permitted.source: `Policy::JLREQ`'s own default answer to `adjustment.remainder` (leading), applied to `docs/decisions/mono-ruby-separation-split.md`'s own even split
the trailing reading `jlreq_unit::RemainderRule::Trailing` permits — a statement to an implementation that declares this alternative; this workspace's own default run does not select it
